{{Short description|Mathematical problem related to equal partitions of measures}}
The '''problem of the Nile''' is a mathematical problem related to equal partitions of [[Measure (mathematics)|measures]]. The problem was first presented by [[Ronald Fisher]] in 1936–1938.<ref>[[Ronald Fisher|R. A. Fisher]]. "[https://digital.library.adelaide.edu.au/dspace/bitstream/2440/15233/1/156.pdf Quelques remarques sur l'estimation en statistique]". Biotypologie, v. 6, 1938, pp. 153–159.

R. A. Fisher. "Uncertain inference". Proc. Amer. Acad. Arts Sci., vol. 77, 1936, pp. 245–257.</ref> It is presented by Dubins and Spanier in the following words:<ref name="DS">{{Cite journal|last1=Dubins|first1=Lester Eli|author1-link=Lester Dubins|last2=Spanier|first2=Edwin Henry|author2-link=Edwin Spanier|year=1961|title=How to Cut a Cake Fairly|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=68|issue=1|pages=1–17|doi=10.2307/2311357|jstor=2311357}}</ref><blockquote>"Each year, the [[Nile]] would flood, thereby irrigating or perhaps devastating parts of the agricultural land of a [[Prehistoric Egypt|predynastic Egyptian]] village. The value of different portions of the land would depend upon the height of the flood. In question was the possibility of giving to each of the ''k'' residents, piece of land whose value would be 1/''k'' of the total land value, no matter what the height of the flood."</blockquote>Formally, for each height ''h'', there is a [[nonatomic measure]] ''v<sub>h</sub>'' on the land, which represents the land values when the height of the Nile is ''h''.

In general, there can be infinitely many different heights, and hence, infinitely many different measures. [[William Feller]] showed in 1938 that a solution for the general case might not exist.<ref>Note on regions similar to the sample space, Statistical Research Memoirs, Cambridge, 1938, 116–125.</ref>

When the number of different heights (= measures) is finite, a solution always exists. This was first noted by [[Jerzy Neyman]] in 1946, and proved as a corollary of the [[Dubins–Spanier theorems]] in 1961. The problem in this case is called the '''[[exact division]]''' or '''consensus division''' problem.

== Related problems ==
A related problem is the '''problem of similar regions''' studied by [[Jerzy Neyman|Neyman]] and [[Egon Pearson|Pearson]].<ref>J. Neyman and E. S. Pearson, "On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses", Philos. Trans. Roy. Soc. London. Ser A, vol. 231, 1932–33, pp. 289–377 (Separately as A 702).</ref> Here, instead of partitioning the land into ''k'' subsets, one only looks for a ''single'' subset, whose value for each measure ''v<sub>h</sub>''  is ''r'' times the total value (where ''r'' is a given constant in [0,1]). From existence perspective, the problem is equivalent to the problem of the Nile, as noted by [[Georges Darmois]].<ref>G. Darmois, "Resumes exhaustifs et probleme du Nil", C.R. Acad. Sci. Paris, vol. 222, 1946, pp 266–268.</ref>  However, they differ in the number of required cuts. The optimal number of required cuts for any ''r'' is described in the [[Stromquist–Woodall theorem]].
